claims.text: The proposed computational method is based on density functional theory with phonon-dispersion calculations.
The proposed method can accurately identify high-entropy alloys with low phonon thermal conductivity.
The target materials are high-entropy alloys in an initial, unprocessed state.
Phonon dispersion and phonon density of states are the structural mediators used to predict phonon thermal conductivity.
Ab initio calculations can predict the phonon thermal conductivity of high-entropy alloys.
Predicting phonon thermal conductivity enables identification of high-entropy alloys having low phonon thermal conductivity.
The proposed method will identify low-phonon-conductivity high-entropy alloys more accurately than current predictive approaches.
More accurate identification of low-phonon-conductivity high-entropy alloys will lead to better thermal-insulation performance.
The method's applicability is limited to high-entropy alloys and thermal-insulation applications.
The method's accuracy depends on the quality of its input data.
The method's accuracy depends on the complexity of the high-entropy-alloy system.
Mean absolute error against experimental phonon thermal conductivity can be used to compare the proposed method with current predictive approaches.
Failure to show a significant accuracy improvement over current approaches would falsify the hypothesis.
An MAE below 10% is given as an example criterion in the falsification rule.

contradictions.description: The falsification rule says that lack of significant improvement falsifies the hypothesis but then gives 'MAE < 10%' as its example. A low MAE ordinarily indicates good accuracy rather than failure, and the rule does not clarify whether 10% refers to absolute normalized error or improvement relative to the baseline.
